course.title: Parsing and Serialization
course.description: Every system boundary is a parser. The HTTP request, the CSV export from finance, the config file, the message on a queue, the row written by last year's version of your code: each arrives as text or bytes and has to become data you can trust, and each has to be written back so the next reader gets exactly what you meant. Most production bugs at boundaries are not exotic. A comma in a name splits a field, a trailing empty field disappears, a quote is not escaped, a line arrives in two TCP reads, or an old record has one field fewer than the reader expects. This module builds the small parsers and writers you will otherwise reach for `split` to fake: a lexer, a quoted-CSV reader, a validating config loader, a line-protocol framer, a JSON writer and reader, a versioned record format, and a property test that proves a codec round trips.

lessons.title: Parsing and Serialization
lessons.explanation:
# 18 · Parsing and Serialization

Every system boundary is a parser. The HTTP request, the CSV export from
finance, the config file, the message on a queue, the row written by
last year's version of your code: each arrives as text or bytes and has
to become data you can trust, and each has to be written back so the
next reader gets exactly what you meant. Most production bugs at
boundaries are not exotic. A comma in a name splits a field, a trailing
empty field disappears, a quote is not escaped, a line arrives in two
TCP reads, or an old record has one field fewer than the reader expects.
This module builds the small parsers and writers you will otherwise
reach for `split` to fake: a lexer, a quoted-CSV reader, a validating
config loader, a line-protocol framer, a JSON writer and reader, a
versioned record format, and a property test that proves a codec round
trips.

## The mental model

### 1 · Lex, then parse, and always know where you are

A parser reads with ONE position that only moves forward. Splitting the
work in two keeps both halves simple: the **lexer** turns characters into
tokens (and throws away spaces), and the **parser** turns tokens into
structure. Whoever finds a problem knows the offset, so the error can say
*where*:

```
tokenize("x <= 3.5")   → IDENT x @0 · OP <= @2 · NUMBER 3.5 @5
parse("[1 2]")         → "unexpected '2' at 3"
                                       ^ the reader can find this
```

Two habits make lexers correct. **Maximal munch**: always take the
longest token (`<=` is one operator, not `<` then `=`). And **decide by
looking at one char**: a digit starts a number, a `"` starts a string,
a `{` starts an object. Recursive descent is the same idea for nested
data: one method per grammar rule, each calling the others.

### 2 · Quoting is a state machine, not a split

`line.split(",")` is correct until the first customer called
"Smith, J". Real formats have a quoting rule, and the parser has to know
at every char whether it is inside quotes:

```
 7,"Smith, J","say ""hi"""
 │ └─ quoted: commas are data, "" is one "
 └─ unquoted: runs to the next comma
```

The same applies on the way out. A writer that builds JSON with string
concatenation produces broken output for the first name containing a
quote, and a security hole for the first one containing `","admin":true`.
**Escape on write, unescape on read, and do both in one place.**

### 3 · Framing: where does one message end?

TCP and files give you a stream of bytes, not messages. One read can
hold half a message or three of them. Protocols pick a framing rule:

| framing | how a message ends | seen in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| delimiter | a line end (`\n` or `\r\n`) | SMTP, Redis RESP, IRC, NDJSON logs |
| length prefix | the header says how many bytes follow | HTTP `Content-Length`, Kafka, gRPC |
| self-describing | the parser knows when the value is complete | JSON in a stream, CBOR |

A decoder keeps the unfinished frame BETWEEN reads, and it needs a
maximum frame length, or a client that never sends `\n` makes you buffer
forever (Netty's `LineBasedFrameDecoder` takes `maxLength` for exactly
this reason).

### 4 · Data outlives code: version everything you store

The bytes written today will be read by code written next year. Put a
version in every record, have the writer write only the latest version,
and have the reader **migrate step by step** (v1 → v2 → v3). Each step
knows only its neighbour, so v4 is one more step, not a rewrite.

```
"1;Ada Lovelace;ada@x"   ─v1→v2─►  "2;Ada Lovelace;ada@x;N"  ─v2→v3─►  User(Ada, Lovelace, ada@x, false)
```

Protobuf, Avro and database migrations are this idea with tooling.

### 5 · The one law: decode(encode(x)) == x

Every codec has a round-trip law, and **property-based testing** checks
it on hundreds of generated inputs instead of the five you thought of. A
seeded generator makes every failure replayable; **shrinking** cuts a
random failure down to the smallest input that still fails, which usually
names the bug by itself (`[]` encodes like `[""]`; `[";"]` is not
escaped).

## The details that bite

1. **`"a;b;;".split(";")` returns `[a, b]`.** `split` drops trailing
   empty strings. Use `split(";", -1)` whenever empty fields are legal
   (exercise 07).
2. **Split at the FIRST separator** when the value may contain it:
   `url=http://h/?a=b` has two `=` (`indexOf`, not `split`) (exercise
   03).
3. **Line numbers count every line**, blank lines and comments too, or
   they do not match the operator's editor (exercise 03).
4. **`Boolean.parseBoolean("yes")` is `false` and never throws.**
   Validate booleans yourself (exercise 03).
5. **A `"` after a closing quote is malformed, not data.** Accepting
   `"ab"c` hides broken exports (exercise 02).
6. **Never split a CSV into lines first**: a quoted field may contain a
   newline (exercise 02).
7. **Strip the `\r` of a CRLF only when the `\n` arrives**; it may come
   in the previous read (exercise 04).
8. **Check the frame length as you buffer**, not when the line ends, or
   memory is unbounded (exercise 04).
9. **Every char below U+0020 must be escaped in a JSON string**, not
   just `\n` and `\t` (exercise 05).
10. **`instanceof Number` lets `Double` in**: dispatch on the exact types
    you support and refuse the rest (exercise 05).
11. **After the top-level value only whitespace may follow**, or `{} {}`
    parses (exercise 06).
12. **`Long.parseLong` overflow is a `NumberFormatException`**; turn it
    into an error with a position (exercise 06).
13. **Terminate, don't separate**: with separators `[]` and `[""]` are
    the same text (exercise 08).
14. **A codec that throws is failing**, not passing, in a property test
    (exercise 08).
15. **Java parses `\u` escapes even in comments.** A comment containing
    a backslash, `u` and then non-hex characters is a compile error.
    Write "backslash-u" in prose.

## Cheat table

| task | reach for | not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| split keeping empty fields | `s.split(";", -1)` | `s.split(";")` |
| split once | `int i = s.indexOf('='); s.substring(0, i)` | `s.split("=")[1]` |
| parse an int, collecting errors | `try { Integer.parseInt(v) } catch (NumberFormatException e)` | letting it escape |
| build output | one `StringBuilder` passed down | `+` in a recursive method |
| four hex digits | `String.format("\\u%04x", (int) c)` | `Integer.toHexString(c)` (no padding) |
| ordered map from parsing | `LinkedHashMap` | `HashMap` (order lost), `Map.of` (no nulls) |
| reproducible random input | `new Random(seed)` | `new Random()`, `Math.random()` |

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-tokenizer.java` | ★☆☆ | a lexer with maximal munch and error offsets |
| 02 | `02-csv-records.java` | ★★☆ | an RFC 4180 CSV reader: quotes, doubled quotes, newlines in fields |
| 03 | `03-config-file.java` | ★★☆ | a typed key=value config loader that reports every error with its line |
| 04 | `04-line-framing.java` | ★★☆ | a line-protocol decoder over partial reads, CRLF and a max frame length |
| 05 | `05-json-writer.java` | ★★☆ | a JSON writer for a fixed subset with correct escaping |
| 06 | `06-json-reader.java` | ★★★ | a recursive-descent JSON reader with exact error positions |
| 07 | `07-versioned-records.java` | ★★☆ | a versioned record format with step-by-step migration |
| 08 | `08-round-trip-properties.java` | ★★★ | an escaping codec plus a seeded property checker that shrinks failures |

Do the warm-ups and core in order. Stretch if time allows. 05 and 06 are
a pair: write JSON, then read it back. 06 and 01 are the same technique
at two sizes. If you did module 06 (`05-csv-store`), compare its naive
CSV with exercise 02; if you did module 12, exercise 04 is how the bytes
of a message become a message, and exercise 07 is how a consumer reads
an event written by an older producer.

---

javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.instructions:
**Concepts:** lexing · maximal munch · token positions · error offsets  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

Every parser starts with a lexer: it turns characters into tokens so
the parser never thinks about spaces again. Write tokenize(src):
  NUMBER  digits, optionally "." and at least one more digit ("3.14")
  IDENT   a letter or "_", then letters, digits or "_"
  OP      + - * / ( ) = < >  and the two-char  == <= >= !=
Spaces, tabs and newlines separate tokens and are skipped. pos is the
0-based offset of the token's first char. Take the LONGEST operator
("<=" is one token). Any other char, a lone "!", a "." that does not
sit between digits of ONE number: IllegalArgumentException "unexpected
'c' at N" (N is that char's offset). "12ab" is a NUMBER then an IDENT.

    tokenize("x <= 3.5") → [IDENT "x" @0, OP "<=" @2, NUMBER "3.5" @5]
    tokenize("a + $b")   → IllegalArgumentException "unexpected '$' at 4"

hint: one index, one loop; decide the token kind from the current char.
javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.explanation:
A lexer is one index walking the string. The current char decides the
token kind: a digit starts a NUMBER, a letter or "_" an IDENT, an
operator char an OP. Each branch consumes as many chars as belong to
the token and records where it STARTED, so later errors can point at
the source ("line 3, col 7" in a real compiler is the same offset).
Operators use maximal munch: look one char ahead and take the
two-char operator if it exists. That is why "<=" is one token and
"a=<b" is "=", "<". "!" exists only as the start of "!=".
The classic wrong turn is accepting "3." or a second "." as part of a
number; then "1.2.3" lexes as one token and the parser downstream gets
garbage. A "." is only consumed when a digit follows it, and only
once per number; any other "." falls through to the error branch,
which reports the char and its offset.
Java detail: Character.isDigit accepts non-ASCII digits like '٣';
a real lexer compares with '0'..'9' as here.

javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.instructions:
**Concepts:** CSV (RFC 4180) · quoting · state machines · error offsets  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

line.split(",") breaks on the first customer called "Smith, J". Write
parse(text) → records → fields, the RFC 4180 way:
- fields are separated by ","; spaces are kept, nothing is trimmed;
- a field that STARTS with " is quoted: it runs to the closing quote,
  "" inside it is one ", and commas and newlines in it are literal;
  right after the closing quote must come ",", a line end, or the end;
- a record ends at "\n" or "\r\n" outside quotes; a final line end
  adds no record; "" has no records; an empty line is one empty field.
Errors, IllegalArgumentException with a 0-based offset into text:
  "unterminated quote at N"  (N = the opening quote)
  "unexpected 'c' at N"      (after a closing quote, or a " inside an
                              unquoted field)

    parse("id,name\n7,\"Smith, J\"") → [[id, name], [7, Smith, J]]
    parse("\"say \"\"hi\"\"\",x")    → [[say "hi", x]]

hint: at each field start, look at one char: quoted or not decides all.
javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.explanation:
CSV is not "split on commas"; it is a tiny state machine. At the start
of every field one char decides everything: a " means a quoted field,
anything else an unquoted one. A quoted field is read char by char to
the closing quote, turning "" into one " and treating commas and
newlines as plain data; an unquoted field runs to the next comma or
line end. After the field the next char is the separator: "," starts
another field, a line end closes the record, the end of text closes
everything.
Two wrong turns. Splitting the text into lines FIRST breaks every
quoted field that contains a newline (addresses, comments), so the
record split has to happen inside the same loop. And forgetting the
check after a closing quote silently accepts "ab"c as abc; RFC 4180
says it is malformed, and a parser that guesses hides bad exports.
Errors carry the offset where things went wrong (for an unterminated
quote the OPENING quote, because that is where the reader must look).
Edge cases worth a test of their own: "" (no records), "\n" (one empty
field), a trailing comma (one more empty field).

Parsing that stops at the first error is fine for a compiler run in a
loop, but a config file is fixed by a tired operator at 3 a.m.: give
them every problem at once. So nothing here throws; each check appends
"line N: ..." to a list and moves on, and the good entries are kept.
The line number is the index + 1 of the RAW line, counted before blank
lines and comments are skipped, so it matches what an editor shows.
Split at the FIRST "=" (indexOf, not split("=")): values like URLs
contain "=" too. A map from key to the line where it first appeared
gives the duplicate message its "(first on line M)" and also answers
"did this key appear?" for the required-key check, which is why a key
with a bad value is not reported missing as well.
Java traps: Integer.parseInt throws NumberFormatException (catch it,
do not let one bad line kill the load); Boolean.parseBoolean never
throws and turns "yes" into false, so compare with "true"/"false"
yourself; and Set.of has no order, so sort the missing keys.

javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.instructions:
**Concepts:** framing · partial reads · CRLF · max frame length  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

TCP delivers bytes, not messages: one read can hold half a line or
three lines. Redis, SMTP and IRC frame messages with line ends. Build
LineDecoder(maxLength):
- feed(chunk) returns the frames COMPLETED by this chunk, in order;
  a frame ends at "\n", which is not part of it; a "\r" right before
  the "\n" is dropped too, even if it came in an earlier chunk; any
  other "\r" is data. An empty line is the frame "".
- a frame longer than maxLength (not counting that CR) is DROPPED:
  discard everything up to and including its "\n", add 1 to dropped(),
  and never hold more than maxLength + 1 chars while you do.
- buffered() is how many chars are held for the unfinished frame
  (0 while discarding).
encode(frame) returns frame + "\n"; a frame holding "\n" or "\r":
IllegalArgumentException.

    feed("hel") → []    feed("lo\r") → []    feed("\nhi\n") → [hello, hi]

hint: count the over-long frame when you START discarding it.
javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.explanation:
A stream socket gives you bytes in whatever pieces the network chose,
so a decoder keeps state BETWEEN reads: the unfinished frame. Each
char is either "\n" (the frame is done: emit it, minus one trailing
"\r") or data (append it). Because the "\r" is only stripped when the
"\n" arrives, a CRLF split across two reads still works, and a "\r"
in the middle of a line stays data.
The second job is defence. Without a limit, a client that never sends
"\n" makes the server buffer forever: that is a memory-exhaustion
attack, and why Netty's LineBasedFrameDecoder takes a maxLength. The
moment the content passes maxLength, clear the buffer, count the
frame as dropped ONCE, and switch to discarding until the next "\n".
That keeps memory bounded at maxLength + 1 (room for a final CR).
The classic wrong turn is checking the length only when the "\n"
arrives: correct output, unbounded memory. The other is counting the
drop per chunk instead of per frame.
encode is the other half of the contract: a frame that contains a line
break would be split in two by the reader, so it is refused.

javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.instructions:
**Concepts:** serialization · string escaping · recursion · type dispatch  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

"{\"name\":\"" + name + "\"}" works until a user is called Bob "The
Builder". Write toJson(value) for a fixed subset, compact (no spaces):
  null → null    Boolean → true/false    Integer, Long → 42
  String → "..." with escapes: " → \"   \ → \\   newline → \n
           CR → \r   tab → \t   any other char below U+0020 → the
           6-char escape: backslash, "u", 4 lowercase hex digits
           (U+001F → backslash u001f); every other char as-is
  List → [a,b]   Map with String keys → {"k":v} in the map's own
           iteration order (do not sort)
Anything else (Double, Short, a non-String key, ...), at any depth:
IllegalArgumentException "unsupported type: <SimpleName>".

    toJson(Map.of("ok", List.of(1, true)))  → {"ok":[1,true]}
    toJson("say \"hi\"")                    → "say \"hi\""

hint: one recursive method; a StringBuilder passed down the recursion.
javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.explanation:
A serializer is a recursive walk with one case per supported type,
appending to one shared StringBuilder (building strings per level and
concatenating them is quadratic for deep data). Containers recurse;
scalars print; the final else refuses, so an unexpected type deep in
a structure fails loudly instead of being written as its toString()
("java.lang.Object@1b6d3586" is valid inside quotes and still wrong).
Escaping is where hand-written JSON breaks. A string must escape the
quote and the backslash (or the string ends early), the common
controls get their short forms, and every other char below U+0020 is
illegal raw inside a JSON string, so it gets the 6-char escape
(backslash, "u", 4 hex digits). Non-ASCII text is legal as-is.
Map keys are strings in JSON, so they go through the same escaping;
a non-String key is refused rather than silently turned into "1".
Order: JSON objects are unordered, but writing in the map's own
iteration order keeps output stable for a LinkedHashMap or TreeMap.
Java detail: test Integer and Long explicitly; a check like
"instanceof Number" would let Double through and print 1.0E10.

javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.instructions:
**Concepts:** recursive descent · lookahead · escapes · error positions  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

Write parse(json) for the subset of exercise 05, as a recursive-
descent parser. Results: Map (LinkedHashMap, keys in input order),
List, String, Long, Boolean, null.
- whitespace (space, tab, LF, CR) may surround any token; after the
  one top-level value only whitespace may follow;
- strings: escapes \" \\ \/ \n \r \t and backslash-u + 4 hex digits
  (either case); a raw char below U+0020 inside a string is an error;
- numbers: optional "-", then "0" or digits not starting with 0; no
  fraction or exponent; beyond long: "number out of range at N"
  (N = where the number starts);
- a key that repeats in one object: "duplicate key \"k\" at N"
  (N = its opening quote).
Every other error: IllegalArgumentException "unexpected 'c' at N",
or "unexpected end at N" when the text runs out (N = its length).
Offsets are 0-based.

    parse("{\"a\": [1, true]}") → {a=[1, true]}
    parse("[1 2]")              → "unexpected '2' at 3"

hint: one method per grammar rule; each reads from a shared position.
javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.explanation:
Recursive descent mirrors the grammar: value() looks at ONE char and
dispatches to object(), array(), string(), number() or a literal;
object() and array() call value() for their elements, which is all
the recursion there is. Every method reads from one shared position,
so whoever detects a problem knows exactly where it is: an error
message "at 37" is worth more than any amount of "invalid JSON".
Two helpers keep the error rules in one place: peek() reports
"unexpected end" when the text has run out, and expect(c) reports
"unexpected 'x'" at the offending char.
The traps are at the edges. The top-level value must be followed by
nothing but whitespace, or "{} {}" and "1 x" parse as valid. A number
stops at the first non-digit, so "01" and "1.5" are caught by
whoever reads the NEXT char. Long.parseLong throws on overflow; turn
that into an error at the number's start instead of letting a
NumberFormatException escape. A repeated key is ambiguous (parsers
disagree on which one wins, which attackers exploit), so refuse it.
Java detail: Map.of refuses null values; a JSON null value needs a
LinkedHashMap, which also keeps the keys in input order.

javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.instructions:
**Concepts:** schema versions · migrations · split limits · round trips  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

The user file has lived through three formats, and old lines never get
rewritten. Fields are ";"-separated; the first field is the version:
  v1  "1;fullName;email"
  v2  "2;fullName;email;optIn"         optIn is "Y" or "N"
  v3  "3;first;last;email;optIn"
decode(line) returns a v3 User by migrating step by step: v1 → v2
sets optIn N; v2 → v3 splits fullName at the FIRST space (first =
before it, last = everything after; no space: last is ""). Empty
fields are legal, trailing ones too ("1;Prince;" has email "").
encode(user) always writes v3; upgrade(line) = encode(decode(line)).
Errors (IllegalArgumentException): "unknown version 'x'";
"version N expects M fields, got K" (counting the version field);
"bad opt-in 'x'"; encode of a field holding ";" or a line break.

    decode("1;Ada Lovelace;ada@x") → User[Ada, Lovelace, ada@x, false]
    upgrade("2;Cher;c@x;Y")        → "3;Cher;;c@x;Y"

hint: what does "a;b;;".split(";") return? Read split's javadoc.
javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.explanation:
Stored data outlives the code that wrote it, so every record carries
its version and the reader migrates OLD to NEW one step at a time:
v1 → v2 → v3. Each step is small and knows only its neighbour, so
adding v4 later means one more step, not a rewrite of every reader.
The writer only ever writes the latest version; "upgrade" is just
decode then encode, which is how a background job rewrites old rows.
The Java trap is String.split: "1;Prince;".split(";") drops trailing
empty strings and returns 2 fields, so a legal record with an empty
email looks malformed (or worse, a short record looks fine). The
limit -1 keeps every field. Count fields per version BEFORE indexing.
The migration trap is splitting the name with split(" "): "Grace
Brewster Hopper" would lose a part. indexOf(' ') splits once, and the
"no space" case (Cher) needs an explicit last name of "".
Finally, the writer guards the format: a ";" inside a field would
shift every later field when read back, so encode refuses it, and the
round-trip test decode(encode(u)) == u pins the whole contract.

javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.instructions:
**Concepts:** escaping · property tests · seeded generators · shrinking  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

1) A codec for a list of strings: encode writes each item with "\" →
"\\" and ";" → "\;", followed by ";" ([] → "", [""] → ";"). decode
inverts it; IllegalArgumentException, offsets 0-based: a "\" at the
very end: "dangling escape at N"; "\" + any other char: "bad escape
at N" (N = the "\"); text after the last ";": "unterminated item at
N" (N = where that item starts).
2) findCounterexample(enc, dec, seed, trials) hunts for an input
where dec(enc(x)) is not x (or either throws a RuntimeException).
Generate with new Random(seed): per trial size = nextInt(5), then per
item its length = nextInt(4), then per char one of the 4 chars a ;
backslash b, picked by nextInt(4) (in Java: "a;\\b"). On the
first failure, SHRINK: try removing each item (index ascending), then
each char of each item (item, then char, ascending); take the first
candidate that still fails and start over; stop when none fails.
Return the shrunk input, or empty if all trials pass.

    encode(List.of("a", "b;c")) → "a;b\;c;"
    findCounterexample(join-with-";" codec, ...) → Optional[[]]

hint: a failing case is only useful once it is small enough to read.
javabootcamp/18-parsing-and-serializatio.explanation:
Every serializer has one law: decode(encode(x)) == x. Example tests
check the cases you thought of; a PROPERTY test checks the law on
hundreds of generated inputs, including the ones you did not think
of. This is what jqwik and QuickCheck do, in thirty lines.
The codec itself: TERMINATE each item instead of separating them, so
[] ("") and [""] (";") are different texts, and escape the two special
chars, backslash first in the reader's eyes: "\" always starts a
two-char escape. The join codec in the tests shows the classic bug:
[] and [""] both become "", and a ";" inside an item splits it.
The generator uses a SEEDED Random and a tiny alphabet that is mostly
special chars, so bugs show up in a few trials and a failure can be
replayed exactly from its seed. Shrinking is what makes the result
readable: a random failure like ["b;a", "\\a", ";"] is greedily cut
down (drop an item, else drop a char, keep any cut that still fails)
until no single cut fails. That minimal case ([] or [";"]) names the
bug by itself. Wrong turns: shrinking a copy you then throw away,
restarting the generator instead of the shrink loop, and treating an
exception from the codec as a pass instead of a failure.
